Andrew Nassar, CTO of IC Realtime – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2220 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the firm through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis.
  • IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments.
  • You’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the firm through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis. With more than 20 years in the surveillance industry, he focuses on turning advances in computer vision and edge computing into practical tools for understanding events, finding footage, and improving security operations.

IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments. Its Bunker platform adds AI analysis to compatible camera systems through a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson-powered gateway, supporting contextual alerts and natural-language video search. The platform combines local analysis with cloud-connected services for remote access and video history.

You’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI. What convinced you that AI could fundamentally change surveillance, and what advances have made sophisticated video analysis practical at the edge?

It has been revealed that we have worked with machine learning and computer vision on our cameras for years. The opportunity became much more useful when the system could help someone understand an event and find the relevant footage, rather than simply produce more video to review. A homeowner wants to know what deserves attention. A business wants to find an incident without spending hours searching.

Bunker brings that approach to a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson gateway at the property. Moving core analysis closer to the cameras can reduce the dependence on sending every analytical task to the cloud and improve responsiveness. The practical advance is the combination of local computing and software that turns video into contextual alerts and searchable events.

Industry observers note that my standard is still proven value. The technology has to solve a real problem in the environment where the customer will use it. A good demonstration is the beginning of that process.

Using Bunker as an example, could you walk us through what happens between a camera capturing an event and a user receiving an alert? Which AI functions run locally, what still requires the cloud, and what data leaves the property?

At a high level, a compatible camera sends video to the Bunker Gateway, and core AI analysis happens on that gateway at the property. The platform links detected activity to video events and can send a contextual alert with a snapshot and a plain-language description. The user can then review the video in the app.

Recent findings suggest that bunker uses a hybrid architecture. Cloud connectivity supports remote access, subscription services and video history, so it would be misleading to call the platform cloud-free or to say no video leaves the property. What matters is how that data is protected when it does leave. Everything is encrypted in transit, including live video, which stays encrypted from the gateway all the way to the viewer’s screen. The infrastructure in between relays it but can’t watch it. Each gateway authenticates with its own certificate, never shared credentials, and footage stored in the cloud is encrypted.

Customers should get a clear explanation of that flow, including which features depend on the internet and what happens when the connection is down.

Security cameras operate in rain, darkness, glare, and constantly changing environments. What is the hardest real-world failure you’ve encountered, and how do you measure whether improvements reduce false alarms without increasing missed incidents?

In a recent development, I’ve been in this industry for more than 20 years, and camera technology has improved dramatically, especially in low light and difficult conditions. Nighttime and noisy images are now nearly as clear as daytime. Even so, rain, glare, fog and snow can still reduce an AI model’s accuracy. Better sensors don’t remove those variables.

So we chose a dynamic approach that adjusts to changing environments and times of day, rather than relying on one fixed configuration. Over the past two years of development, we’ve put thousands of hours into testing in real-world installations, not just cameras on a bench, and we’ve built the system around what those deployments taught us.

Sources indicate that I wouldn’t judge an improvement by a lower notification count alone. The question is whether it removes irrelevant alerts while still catching the incidents that matter. Reducing noise is only valuable if the system stays useful when something important happens.

Detecting a person or vehicle is different from deciding that behavior is concerning. How do you define an anomaly, adapt that definition to each location, and prevent the system from treating harmless activity as a threat?

A detected object does not, by itself, tell you whether there is a problem. A delivery at the front entrance and activity in a restricted area can involve the same type of object but require very different responses. The starting point should be the customer’s use case and the context of that particular property.

Industry observers note that I would distinguish an event worth reviewing from a conclusion that someone is a threat. The system should help a person understand what was observed and why it was surfaced, with access to the underlying footage. It should not encourage the user to treat every unfamiliar activity as evidence of wrongdoing.

Recent findings suggest that as these systems become more capable, the challenge is to make that context useful without overstating what the AI knows. Human judgment remains crucial, particularly when an alert could lead to a consequential action.

It has been revealed that natural-language search promises to replace hours of manually reviewing footage. How does your system connect a user’s description to the right video, and how do you test for missed events, incorrect matches, or AI-generated descriptions that the footage doesn’t support?

In a recent development, the concept is to make video searchable in the language a person would naturally use. As activity is detected, Bunker creates time-stamped descriptions associated with video events. A user’s question is used to search that indexed record and surface relevant footage. That gives the user a starting point without manually scrubbing through the entire recording.

The footage should remain the basis for checking the result. A generated description is useful for navigation, but it should not be treated as more authoritative than what the camera actually captured.

In a recent development, for testing, I would separate three questions: Did the system miss a relevant event? Did it retrieve something that does not match the request? Did the description include something the footage does not support? Those are different failure modes. Evaluating only whether the search returns a plausible-looking answer would not be enough.

Industry observers note that what trade-offs does NVIDIA Jetson hardware impose on model size, accuracy, power consumption, and the number of camera feeds you can analyze? How do you maintain reliable performance when using older third-party cameras, reaching processing capacity, or losing internet connectivity?

According to recent reports, the design question is how to deliver useful analysis within the resources available at the property. Model complexity, the amount of video being processed and the required response time all have to fit the gateway’s operating limits. That is why the number of supported streams alone does not tell the whole performance story.

Bunker’s launch plans support up to 10 camera streams. Compatible ONVIF cameras let customers keep their existing hardware, but compatibility still needs to be verified for each installation. Profiles, firmware, image quality and the features being used all matter.

Recent findings suggest that we also need to be precise about resilience. Local processing and cloud-connected services are different parts of the system, and having an edge gateway doesn’t mean every feature works normally during an internet outage. Updates are part of reliability too. Every enhancement is signed and verified on the gateway before it installs, older vulnerable versions are rejected, and a failed update rolls back automatically. A bad update shouldn’t be what takes a property’s security system offline.

Local inference alone doesn’t answer every privacy question. Where does Bunker store footage, search queries, and AI-generated metadata, how long are they retained, and who can access them? How do you improve your models without assuming access to customers’ private footage?

Footage and the databases behind the service are encrypted at rest. Passwords are hashed and sessions expire, so even a database breach wouldn’t give anyone working logins. The gateway itself is encrypted too, so a stolen device yields no footage and no credentials. Bunker’s launch offering included 60 days of cloud video history on Standard and 365 days on Premium, plus Video Vault for clips a customer chooses to save.

We don’t use customer footage to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates of anyone the cameras capture. A customer using the product is not permission for us to reuse their private video.

Industry observers note that the controversy surrounding Flock Safety has highlighted questions about who can search surveillance data and whether access is properly revoked. Although your deployment model differs, what lessons apply to your systems, and which safeguards should be mandatory rather than optional?

According to recent reports, the backlash against Flock isn’t really about the AI. It’s about who can get in and search the data. Much of the scrutiny came down to account security, including lawmakers asking why multi-factor authentication wasn’t mandatory. When a stolen password is enough to search a surveillance system, it doesn’t matter where the model runs.

With Bunker, the only people with access to a system’s data are the consumers that system’s owner has granted access. We don’t share it with third parties, we don’t use customer data to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates.

Security has to start at the device and carry through to the account. Every Bunker gateway ships with its own cryptographic identity, so there are no default passwords to change or for an attacker to look up. Firmware is verified at every boot, updates are signed and checked before they install, and logins are protected with multi-factor authentication. Beyond that, access should be removed promptly when it’s no longer needed, and sensitive activity should leave an auditable record. Trust depends on being able to explain who did what.

It has been revealed that people captured by a camera often aren’t the people who bought it. How should AI surveillance account for the privacy of neighbors, employees, visitors, and passersby, and are there capabilities you would deliberately refuse to build?

The installation needs a defined purpose, and that purpose should guide what is captured, what is analyzed and who can see the results. Wanting to secure an entrance doesn’t mean every activity on a neighboring property should become part of a searchable record.

Sources indicate that one line we’ve drawn is identity. Bunker doesn’t create biometric templates, and it doesn’t attach an identity to anyone it detects. It describes what happened, not who someone is. That keeps the system focused on events rather than on tracking or profiling people.

It has been revealed that more capability doesn’t automatically mean more value. If a feature creates a serious trust problem without solving a clear customer problem, that’s a reason not to build it.

Looking ahead three to five years, what meaningful capability do you expect edge AI to unlock beyond today’s detection and search—and what technical or trust problem must be solved before it deserves widespread adoption?

According to recent reports, honestly, the future of AI is uncharted right now, and it’s moving faster than anything I’ve seen in my career. We’re following those changes almost daily and looking at where they can genuinely benefit the people using our platform.

Recent findings suggest that the areas that matter most to us are context, understanding, and systems that keep learning and improving. The value is in helping someone understand a developing situation and decide what needs attention, instead of piecing together a string of separate notifications.

The technical challenge is to do that reliably in changing environments and within the limits of the local hardware. The trust challenge is to make the system’s limits and data practices easy to understand. People need to know what it observed, what it inferred and when a human needs to make the call.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore professional security cameras, recorders, and AI-powered video surveillance systems should visit IC Realtime.

Industry observers note that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

It has been revealed that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS.
  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • Uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond. The hybrid architecture retains translation keys and frequently accessed values in memory while storing the remaining values on disk. The system serves millions of translations per second and maintains a cache hit rate above 99.9%.

The optimization addresses two problems identified through memory profiling across Uber's Go services. Garbage collection (GC) consumed more than 20% of CPU utilization in some services, with translations accounting for approximately 70% of allocated objects.

At Uber's scale, even small inefficiencies in memory management can add up.

The first optimization replaced Go's sync.Map with a conventional map[string]string protected by an RWMutex. The workload was predominantly read-heavy, with infrequent updates and no individual deletions. The previous implementation created multiple objects and pointers for each translation entry, increasing GC overhead. Moving to a value-based map reduced object allocations and improved CPU utilization by more than 30% in the affected service.

In a recent development, however, reducing object allocations did not solve the overall memory consumption problem. Translation datasets could contain two to three million keys, although individual services typically accessed only a small subset. Cache refreshes introduced another glitch: the service built a replacement cache in the background before atomically swapping it with the existing one. Both copies therefore occupied memory simultaneously, causing some services to run out of memory during refreshes.

According to recent reports, uber considered external caching and generating service-specific translation subsets, but both introduced additional operational or maintenance costs. The team instead adopted a hybrid storage design that preserves the existing Get() and Put() API. All keys remain available in memory for fast lookups, while translation values are stored in disk-backed files.

Uber's hybrid translation cache (Source: Uber Blog Post).

Recent findings suggest that the implementation uses 256 shards, each with its own read-write mutex, in-memory entries, and disk file. Six-byte hash-based keys reduce metadata overhead, with a fallback to the original key format to handle collisions. A time-based global least recently used (LRU) policy manages in-memory entries. During cache refreshes, the system uses access history to preload translations accessed within the previous 15 minutes, avoiding a cold cache after the swap.

In one example, a translation dataset that previously consumed approximately 800 MB in memory required around 40 MB for metadata after the redesign. With a configured limit of 50,000 in-memory entries, actual memory consumption typically ranged between 80 MB and 120 MB. In another reported workload, approximately 30,000 of more than four million entries were loaded in memory, while the cache hit rate remained above 99.9%. The p99 latency for disk-backed cache misses stayed below 100 microseconds.

Memory usage decreased from approximately 2.7 GB to 750 MB (Source: Uber Blog Post).

It has been revealed that uber's experience highlights the cost implications of in-memory caching at scale. The team recommends minimizing object references to reduce GC overhead and measuring how frequently cached values are accessed. When only a small proportion of cached data is actively used, a hybrid approach can retain frequently accessed values in memory while moving the rest to disk.

Tech Report: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super notable for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Sources indicate that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That noted, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

Sources indicate that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

It has been revealed that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

According to recent reports, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing indicated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

Sources indicate that the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Huawei used its November 20, 2026 brand event to introduce OSTA (星芒), a upcoming smartphone sub-brand, and launch the O1 Pro as a HarmonyOS AI phone with a starting list price of CNY 5,699.

According to recent reports, the new brand’s first handset makes Huawei’s own software and assistant its defining features. The official product presentation introduces HarmonyOS 7 AI Pioneer Edition and Xiao Xingmang, an OSTA-specific interactive companion form of the Xiaoyi assistant.

Huawei’s Vmall listing labels the O1 Pro as a newly introduced product and lists the 12GB/256GB version at CNY 5,499, a CNY 200 discount from CNY 5,699. The range also offers 12GB/512GB, 16GB/512GB and 16GB/1TB configurations.

Huawei describes an interaction model in which the Xiaoyi AI screen is available immediately when the display is activated, using frequent usage scenarios and habits to present services proactively. Xiaoyi Space draws on likes, favorites and long-term memory, while natural-voice interaction supports continuous conversation and dialect recognition.

The product’s more consequential claim concerns execution. In Huawei’s coffee example, Xiaoyi uses location and preferences to recommend a drink, incorporates discounts and completes the order. Other demonstrations offer restaurant suggestions during travel, return guidance after a concert, meeting-schedule reminders and food-order pickup notifications, extending the assistant from responses into task completion and timely prompts.

It has been revealed that additional Huawei examples connect viewing records to film recommendations and post-viewing discussions, remember food preferences for personalized suggestions, and provide game information and match reminders. Together, those examples place the assistant across entertainment, dining, travel and work, with Xiao Xingmang supplying the companion interface for OSTA users.

Recent findings suggest that the official specifications list a Kirin 9030S processor and HarmonyOS 7.0, alongside a 6.39-inch OLED display with a 16:9.5 aspect ratio, 2232-by-1320 resolution and up to 120Hz refresh. The handset is 6.68mm thick and weighs about 200 grams.

The specifications also list a 7,000mAh typical-capacity battery supporting up to 66W wired and 50W wireless charging, with the chargers required for those maximum rates sold separately. The rear camera system combines a 200-megapixel optically stabilized main camera, a 50-megapixel optically stabilized periscope telephoto camera with approximately 3.7x optical zoom, and Huawei’s second-generation Hongfeng color camera.

Industry observers note that for meeting capture, a four-microphone spatial array supports directional pickup. Huawei says its AI recording functions provide real-time transcription, summaries and translation, giving the phone an administrative use case beyond the consumer-oriented assistant demonstrations. The device also supports eSIM alongside two physical nano-SIM slots, although eSIM use requires carrier service.

It has been revealed that huawei’s footnotes set vital limits on that pitch. The phone ships with HarmonyOS 7, but some functions and cross-device experiences are still being adapted, and certain listed features await a later software upgrade. Dialect recognition right now covers a specified set of regional dialects, with Huawei cautioning that other local variants may be recognized inaccurately.

Recent findings suggest that AI-assisted camera composition must be enabled manually, and pose recommendations work only at the 4x setting in photo and portrait modes. Huawei also identifies AI-assisted recording output as reference material and notes actual performance depends on the application involved. The AI experience therefore varies by feature, application and software readiness.

It has been revealed that OSTA gives Huawei a dedicated consumer brand for making HarmonyOS AI the main reason to choose a handset. The O1 Pro’s most consequential feature is the connection between Xiaoyi’s proactive suggestions and its ability to complete tasks, because that connection distinguishes Huawei’s system-level AI pitch from a phone that merely includes an assistant.

Breaking: Stavros Gadinis, Berkeley Law Professor and Author of Corporate Ordering – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law.
  • His latest book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled.
  • Your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stavros Gadinis is the George R. Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. His research examines corporate governance, financial regulation, and the internal systems companies use to make and monitor decisions. Before entering academia, he practiced corporate law in Europe.

His latest book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled. Through cases involving ridesharing, climate sustainability, and artificial intelligence, it considers how companies make rules, exercise authority, and oversee their own conduct.

Your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law. How did that background shape your thinking, and what inspired you to write Corporate Ordering?

Sources indicate that I began my career practicing corporate law in Europe, and then spent many years at Berkeley studying corporate governance and financial regulation, including how rules spread across borders when no single government is in charge. We tend to think of the business world and the regulatory world as opposites, one eager for quick decisions and large profits, the other committed to bureaucratic process and the public good. Practice and research both taught me that the line is much blurrier than that.

The book grew out of conversations with general counsel and senior executives about how they handle controversial decisions, the ones where employees, customers, communities and governments all want different things. What struck me is how closely their methods resemble those of a good regulator. They gather information by reaching out to the people affected, they explain their choices publicly, and they build mechanisms to check whether those choices hold up. These are not regulatory habits or corporate habits. They are the principles of sound decisionmaking in any institution that wields power over others. Corporate Ordering is my attempt to describe that machinery, show where it works, and show where it fails.

What is “corporate ordering,” and how does it help explain the way AI companies set rules for technologies that regulation has yet to catch up with?

Corporate ordering is the internal governance infrastructure companies build to make contested decisions before the law tells them what to do. It has three functions, which mirror the branches of a state. Rulemaking is how a company writes its own principles. Executive action is how it applies them to concrete decisions. Monitoring is how it checks whether it followed through, and how it finds out when it did not.

AI companies show all three at work. The frontier labs write constitutions, model specifications and safety frameworks, which is rulemaking. They decide whether a model is ready to launch, what it will refuse and who gets access, which is executive action. And they commission red-teaming, outside evaluations and incident reporting, which is monitoring. In the book I chart these functions across the major labs. The differences are real, but so is a striking convergence, as each firm discovers why it needs every piece.

Sources indicate that I want to be clear about one thing, because it is often misread. Corporate ordering is not an argument against regulation. It describes the material regulation will be built from. When legislators act, they borrow concepts the companies developed first. The real question is whether that first draft was written carefully enough to deserve borrowing.

According to recent reports, your book examines ridesharing, climate sustainability, and AI governance. Which lessons from the first two areas are most useful for AI, and where does AI present fundamentally different challenges?

Industry observers note that the lesson from ridesharing and climate is that corporations very often write the first draft of the law. Uber and Lyft developed insurance and safety reporting practices before states had rules for them, and much of corporate carbon accounting runs on the GHG Protocol, a standard business helped build. Regulators then condoned those practices, supplemented them or wrote them into law. Regulation rarely starts from a blank slate. And the more thoughtful companies are about their choices, the more they take affected parties into account, the more likely those choices are to survive into regulation.

AI differs in two ways. The first is speed. Regulators are often a step behind industry, but in AI the gap is far wider. Regulators will have to look to companies to develop standards and internal processes, and concentrate their own efforts on oversight, verification and enforcement. That makes their role different, not smaller. Verification is where public power matters most, because it is where the conflict of interest with management is strongest. The second difference is reach. AI touches nearly every part of daily life, and it has become a major investment for the nation as a whole. The systemic risk implications are as hard to miss as they are to fathom.

When an AI manufacturer selects and pays its own outside safety evaluators, what safeguards make that oversight meaningfully independent?

In a recent development, this conflict of interest is familiar from financial auditing, and corporate law already has tools to manage it. The first is who hires and fires. The relationship with the evaluator should sit with independent directors who have no other financial ties to the company, much as the audit committee, not the CEO or CFO, oversees the external auditor. Management should not be able to dismiss a reviewer whose findings are inconvenient.

In a recent development, the second is access and publication. The evaluator needs to see what it asks to see, and it needs the right to publish its findings, or at least a meaningful summary, without a company veto. Reputational risk is what gives a review its teeth. The third is common review standards, so that an evaluation means the same thing across firms and evaluators cannot compete by being lenient. The fourth is protection for whistleblowers, and even rewards when they bring actionable information, because people inside the company are often the first to know when an evaluation was steered.

Sources indicate that suppose an outside evaluator identifies a serious safety concern just before a major model launch. Who should receive that finding, and who should have the authority to delay or stop deployment?

The finding should go to the board directly, ideally to a committee of independent directors responsible for safety, and not only through the management team that is pushing for the launch. Management can and should respond, but it should not be the filter. The authority to delay or stop deployment should rest with the board, because this is exactly the kind of decision boards exist to make, one with large stakes, conflicting interests and no obvious right answer.

Industry observers note that but the more key point is that the decision must be explicit and documented, and traceable to the people who made it. If the board goes ahead despite the concern, the record should show what it knew, what it weighed and why it judged the risk acceptable. That paper trail creates the conditions for liability, or at least reputational damage, and it makes people think twice. Courts are increasingly willing to recognize that design choices in software have consequences for users, and a company that can show a serious, documented effort stands in a very different position from one that cannot.

When safety concerns conflict with revenue targets or competitive pressure, what should a credible board decision-making process look like?

A credible process is an informed one, and it leaves a record. The board should see concrete information about the costs of delay, the nature and likelihood of the safety concern, and the options for mitigating it. It should ask whether the testing was adequate and, where it was not, commission more or invite outside review. Where real uncertainty remains, there are options between launching and shelving, such as a limited release, a staged rollout or a sandbox, that let the company learn more before it commits. And whatever the board decides, what the company then says publicly about the model’s safety must be accurate, which is where much of the current litigation risk lies.

Then the board should write down what it decided and why. Over time those records become a body of precedent, so the next hard call is measured against the last one, and anyone reviewing the tech giant can see whether its stated principles actually bind. Microsoft has started to build this kind of decision record, and I think it is one of the most underrated tools in AI governance. Competitive pressure is real, and a board may reasonably decide to move ahead. What it cannot do is decide by default.

It has been revealed that your work proposes a “social business judgment” standard for evaluating board decisions. How would that apply to an AI firm that postpones a profitable product launch because of potential public harm?

In a recent development, under existing corporate law, a board that postpones a profitable launch is already well protected. Courts defer to directors’ business judgment, and accepting lower profits today to avoid harm tomorrow fits comfortably within it. The harder question runs the other way, whether the board took public harm seriously at all.

According to recent reports, social business judgment asks the board to evaluate potential public harm the way it evaluates any other business risk, through tangible, measurable and specific metrics wherever possible. The emphasis is on process and due diligence, not on the outcome. A board that sources the right information, hears from those affected and records its reasoning has earned deference, whether it postpones the launch or proceeds with it. A board that does none of this has not. So in the case you describe, the postponement itself is not the issue. The issue is whether the board can show how it reached that decision, and whether it would reach the same one again on the same facts.

AI companies publish safety frameworks and voluntary commitments, but readers rarely see how those policies affect individual decisions. What evidence would distinguish effective governance from a public relations exercise?

Very often, when companies publish frameworks, the public is left wondering whether the framework ever applies to specific decisions or remains rhetoric the company never follows through on. The answer is disclosure of a particular kind. Rather than more statements of principle, companies should report the specific choices they made and how the framework shaped them, which rolls out were delayed, which capabilities were held back, which risk thresholds were triggered and what followed.

Recent findings suggest that the most telling evidence is a decision that cost the manufacturer something. A framework that has never changed an outcome, never delayed a launch and never been invoked against revenue is hard to distinguish from public relations. These disclosures also need to be specific enough to verify, and for the most consequential questions they should be verified by a third party with the standing to say so publicly.

Where does corporate self-governance reach its limits? Which decisions about acceptable AI risk require public rules or democratic oversight?

The most vital limit has to do with failures to monitor. Even a well-intentioned, responsible firm can face a major crisis, and at that moment conflicts of interest multiply. Employees may withhold information that would hurt their jobs or their bonuses. Executives may suppress bad news to avoid public criticism. Fear of lawsuits may keep the company from being open. In past corporate crises, the crucial information usually came from people leadership could not control, external auditors and reviewers, affected parties, or internal whistleblowers using independent reporting channels.

This is where public rules matter most. The law can add relatively little at the rulemaking stage, because statutes tend to borrow their key concepts from the companies. It can add more on disclosure, by reaching firms that will not disclose voluntarily. And it adds the most on verification, by requiring independent review, protecting whistleblowers and giving outside checks real authority.

In a recent development, the other limit is collective. The most a single manufacturer can do is stop itself. It cannot stop its competitors. Decisions about catastrophic risk, including whether to slow the frontier, require coordination across firms and governments, at home and internationally. One model I find promising is an international standard-setter along the lines of the ISSB in sustainability reporting, independent of governments but overseen by trustees that include them. Corporate ordering is necessary for this work, because the taming of these models happens inside the companies that build them, but it cannot carry the work alone.

If you were advising the board of a fast-growing AI organization today, what three governance changes would you prioritize, and what evidence would you look for a year later to determine whether they worked?

First, outreach in rulemaking. Before adopting or revising its safety framework or usage policies, the tech giant should consult the people affected (users, civil society, domain experts) and publish what it heard and how it responded. Second, regular responsibility reporting, an annual account of the hard decisions the board and management made under the framework, with enough detail to be checked. Third, an external monitor, hired by and reporting to independent directors, with full access and the right to publish.

A year later I would look for evidence that each one actually bit. For outreach, at least one rule that changed because of what the organization heard. For reporting, disclosed decisions the company would rather not have discussed, including ones that cost it revenue or time. For the monitor, findings the company did not want, and a record of what the board did about them. If after a year everything reported is good news, the changes have not worked.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore the book and purchase options should visit the official website for Corporate Ordering.

Sources indicate that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

As a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Latest Update: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

It has been revealed that the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to initiative for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Sources indicate that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

According to recent reports, the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many fresh science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

According to recent reports, figure 1. Newly introduced public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an key part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Recent findings suggest that publicly available genomic data has proved notable in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support newly introduced research that others can build upon.

Sources indicate that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

According to recent reports, making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an vital first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

It has been revealed that to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

According to recent reports, the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

In a recent development, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Sources indicate that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or manufacturer building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

Recent findings suggest that we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.
  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.

According to Meta engineers, modern GPU architectures offer advanced performance-optimization features, including warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution, which depart from Triton's traditional programming model, which simplifies kernel development but abstracts away low-level execution structures.

Industry observers note that for example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.

Industry observers note that using these advanced features required "large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code", as they were not readily available as Triton compilers abstractions. To address this challenge, Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to give engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton's programming model.

TLX introduces a latest Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW) execution model that bridges CUDA’s thread-level control and Triton’s block-level abstraction. It extends Triton across five key areas: warp-group orchestration, synchronization, memory orchestration, cluster execution, and optional layout.

It has been revealed that taken together, these capabilities allow TLX to occupy the space between Triton’s productivity and CUDA’s control. Developers retain the advantages of Python, autotuning, and blocked tensor programming while gaining direct access to the execution structures that increasingly determine performance on modern GPUs.

According to recent reports, meta has deployed TLX in production for several months across three major workloads. For GEM model training on thousands of NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, TLX achieved 20–25% end-to-end Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) with up to 2x forward-pass speedup. For In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) in recommendation inference, TLX delivered a 4x speedup on an H100 for a linear compression kernel and reduced compute-intensive net latency up to two-thirds in co-designed models. Finally, in distributed grouped GEMM for LLM pretraining, TLX improved performance, reliability, and maintainability across large GPU fleets for extended training periods.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, AI engineer Kritika Choudary observed:.

When I wrote Flash Attention from scratch in Metal on my M2, the tile loads into threadgroup memory and where to put the barriers were where most of the thinking went, so it's nice to see TLX make that explicit.

On a similar note, Amirul Islam emphasized that:.

Making warp-group handoffs explicit while leaving layouts optional feels like a useful boundary. The producer/consumer pipeline is visible in the source, without forcing every fused stage to start with manual layout bookkeeping.

Meta plans to further expand Triton TLX by adding support for additional NVIDIA, AMD, and custom accelerator architectures, automating warp-group orchestration through higher-level abstractions, and integrating TLX with torch.compile.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI introduced MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry benchmark, on November 20, 2026, and reported that GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh reasoning-effort setting. It tests whether models can connect molecular structures with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds and predict properties.

The other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol. The benchmark addresses a central difficulty in medicinal chemistry: a compound can be potent against a disease-related protein while being poorly absorbed or metabolized too rapidly. Selecting what to test next therefore requires weighing competing properties rather than optimizing one measurement.

The technical paper describes a retrospective set of tasks drawn from 117 papers and patents, encompassing 761 distinct graded molecular structures. Prompts generally stop at a selected decision point in a research program, providing the biological context, earlier compounds and selected experimental findings. Later results are withheld to inform reference answers and grading criteria.

In a recent development, the tasks cover preclinical drug discovery, not clinical development, across seven categories. These include integrated lead selection with 48 tasks, structure–activity relationship forecasting with 26, and smaller groups covering ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion) and delivery, molecular design and enumeration, safety and liabilities, retrosynthesis, and assay biology and mechanism. Eighty-five tasks span more than one scientific-content domain, reflecting how a lead choice can depend simultaneously on potency, selectivity, cell assays, metabolism, exposure and safety.

One problem concerning PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery, asks models to reconstruct three related compounds and predict cellular potency, permeability, efflux and human microsomal clearance. The withheld results illustrate the tradeoff: compound 23 was more potent in cells, while compound 24 crossed a cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in a liver-enzyme assay.

Grading combines deterministic checks with model-judged rubrics. Molecular structure and scientific rationale account for 37.49% and 35.78% of available credit, respectively; ranking and candidate selection account for 17.51%, and numerical or categorical prediction for 8.92%. For structures, RDKit converts submitted SMILES, a text representation of molecular graphs, into canonical isomeric form while preserving stereochemistry and isotopes. Numerical predictions generally receive partial credit based on fold error, while a separate GPT-6 Astra judge at medium reasoning effort scores scientific-rationale criteria as zero, half or full credit.

According to recent reports, across 11 GPT models and 61 model–effort conditions, the paper reports 60,390 graded responses, with ten retained responses for each task in every condition. GPT-6.2 Astra is not among those 11 models; its result comes from the announcement.

Industry observers note that at xhigh, the paper reports that GPT-6 Astra earned 95.37% of available molecular-structure credit and 91.05% of scientific-rationale credit, compared with 50.42% for ranking and candidate selection and 47.02% for numerical prediction. The components cover different applicable tasks and scoring rules, but the results distinguish strong reconstruction and explanation from weaker compound selection and quantitative forecasting.

Sources indicate that A reconstruction task described in the paper makes the structural differences concrete. Models had to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. GPT-6 Astra produced the correct compound in all ten xhigh responses, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed in all ten of theirs. The illustrated Sol answer contained a 15-atom ring, while Luna returned two disconnected fragments. Such errors change the molecule’s identity before any property reasoning begins.

OpenAI states that the scores do not establish whether models can discover upcoming drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Every answer was a single attempt without tools, feedback or new experiments, and the tasks use historical evidence rather than prospective discovery. Prior exposure to the published sources also cannot be ruled out.

In a recent development, for a heuristic check, the authors added source DOI or patent identifiers to all 99 prompts for nine models at xhigh. Mean overall-score changes ranged from a 0.23-percentage-point decrease to a 0.80-point increase, and every model-specific 95% confidence interval included zero. The check cannot establish whether source material appeared in training data.

Sources indicate that the paper describes MedChemBench as close to saturation in its current form and says open-ended design and synthesis grading remains partly tied to reference answers, which may penalize plausible alternatives. Proposed extensions include prospective cases, expert adjudication of alternative answers, explicit treatment of assay uncertainty, and an agent-based track allowing retrieval, calculation, structure verification and multistep revision.

It has been revealed that medChemBench therefore separates chemical comprehension from demonstrated drug-discovery impact. Its strongest results concern reconstructing and explaining fixed historical problems, while compound selection and numerical forecasting lag. The proposed prospective and agent-based evaluations address the resulting open question: whether models can make better research decisions when they must gather evidence, calculate properties and revise their answers over multiple steps.

Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding latest expertise on a single endpoint.

Sources indicate that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

It has been revealed that while we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the fresh multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Web Services released a broad AWS Quick upgrade on November 20, 2026, adding chat-built business workflows and orchestration that pools output from several specialized agents.
  • Recent findings suggest that people can describe a process in chat and have Quick construct a flow that they can run, test, and refine in the same conversation.
  • AWS’s explicitly fictional finance example demonstrates how those pieces fit together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services released a broad AWS Quick upgrade on November 20, 2026, adding chat-built business workflows and orchestration that pools output from several specialized agents. A redesigned web app, new connectors, and expanded administrative controls support a push to make AI-assisted processes repeatable across teams.

Recent findings suggest that people can describe a process in chat and have Quick construct a flow that they can run, test, and refine in the same conversation. A step diagram beside the chat supports review, and flows can coordinate agents, skills, tools, structured data, knowledge, and applications. They can be started from the web, desktop, or mobile. Newly introduced deterministic steps handle fixed calculations and checks alongside agent-led drafting and analysis; AWS says these make repeated workflows consistent and verifiable, with support for longer-running processes and larger data volumes.

AWS’s explicitly fictional finance example demonstrates how those pieces fit together. A monthly reporting flow analyzes regions in parallel, compares results with plan using fixed spreadsheet formulas, applies manager-set thresholds to flag significant variances, and drafts commentary. It then prepares an Excel summary and email for review. A person examines why regions were flagged, requests changes in chat, and approves the report before distribution. Colleagues can subsequently run the same flow, reducing dependence on the original employee’s private checklist.

According to recent reports, pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider, supplied a customer example. Head of Data Rodrigo Marini said nearly four times as many people now work with data each month without expanding the data team, one use case saves 80 hours of work per month, and employees across the business can build agents and flows under shared governance. The result illustrates the release’s central business case: broader participation in data work without matching growth in specialist headcount.

In a recent development, the updated browser home screen combines a prioritized feed of email and messages with a daily briefing. People can ask about an item or have Quick draft a reply for review. Scheduled and longer tasks continue after the browser closes, while Mission Control surfaces completed results and agents awaiting input when users return.

Library collects recent work, favorites, pinned items, and Quick-created files, while conversations, agents, and files synchronize across web, desktop, and mobile. A Customize section brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together, including desktop-built and shared agents and skills. Existing dashboards, topics, and spaces continue working without activation steps.

Multi-agent orchestration lets the agent receiving a request call several specialized agents simultaneously. Each retains its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so domain experts can maintain their own agents; Quick then presents a combined response showing each contribution. In AWS’s shipping-cost example, a forecasting agent using planning data and a procurement agent using vendor contracts address different parts of the same question, leaving the user to decide the next action.

The Meta ads connector uses Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol server for natural-language campaign creation, management, and analysis. Amplitude’s MCP server supports questions about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion. Across connectors, existing access permissions still apply, administrators decide which integrations teams can add, and Quick requires permission for write actions such as creating a Meta campaign or changing a budget.

It has been revealed that reusable skills, previously managed on desktop, can now be browsed, installed, created, and managed in the web app. These instructions capture practices such as checking a contract against a team checklist or formatting a project upgrade.

In a recent development, prompt guardrails are in preview. Administrators can filter content, block prohibited topics and specified words, detect prompt attacks, and protect selected personal-information types. They can test a policy in detect-only mode before enforcing it for individual consumers, identity-provider groups, or the entire account.

Industry observers note that quick adds Japanese, German, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, and Vietnamese. AWS notes the features are available immediately in every Region where Quick is offered, and that customer data remains in the customer’s environment and is not used to train anyone else’s models.

Wider automation therefore comes with explicit operating boundaries: group permissions, connector restrictions, write approvals, and human review define what agents and flows may do when organizations extend Quick across teams.

#46519. Transformers Model Integration Contracts
