    IoT and AI Together: How to Turn Device Data into Better Decisions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Many factories, warehouses and logistics fleets already have sensors.
    • Combining the Internet of Things (IoT) with AI closes that gap.
    • IoT supplies the signal: temperature, vibration, location, energy use, machine status and more, streamed from devices in the field.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Many factories, warehouses and logistics fleets already have sensors. Fewer have a clear way to use what those sensors collect. Dashboards fill up with numbers, and teams still make decisions by instinct. The gap is rarely the hardware. It is the step between raw data and action.

    Combining the Internet of Things (IoT) with AI closes that gap.

    IoT supplies the signal: temperature, vibration, location, energy use, machine status and more, streamed from devices in the field.

    AI supplies the interpretation. It can spot patterns a person would miss, flag unusual readings and predict problems before they happen.

    Recent findings suggest that on their own, sensors tell you what happened. Together with AI, the system can tell you what is likely to happen next and what to do about it.

    In a recent development, practical use cases Predictive maintenance: vibration or temperature trends can warn that a machine is drifting toward failure, so repairs happen on your schedule instead of after a breakdown. Quality control: computer vision on a production line can catch defects that tired human eyes miss. Logistics: location and condition data from vehicles and shipments can drive route and delivery decisions. Energy management: usage patterns can show where power is being wasted. The building blocks of a working system.

    Devices and connectivity. Sensors and gateways that send reliable data, even on poor networks.

    Data pipeline. A way to clean, store and organize readings. Poor data quality is the most common reason these projects stall.

    According to recent reports, models. Anomaly detection, forecasting or vision models, matched to the actual decision you want to improve.

    It has been revealed that edge versus cloud. Some decisions, such as stopping a machine, need to happen locally in milliseconds. Others, such as weekly trend analysis, suit the cloud. Most real systems use both.

    Sources indicate that action layer. Alerts, work orders or automated responses that reach the people who can act.

    Industry observers note that how to avoid a stalled pilot Start from a business question ("Why do we lose hours to unplanned downtime?") rather than a technology. Pilot on one line, one site or one fleet segment. Agree on a measurable outcome before building. Plan for security from day one: device authentication, encrypted data and access control. Make sure the people on the floor trust and understand the output. Conclusion.

    In a recent development, ioT gives you the data, and AI makes it useful. The companies that benefit most don't start with the biggest deployment. They pick one costly problem, prove value quickly, and scale what works.

    About the author: This article was written by the team at Movenetics Digital, which develops AI-powered IoT solutions that connect devices, collect real-time data and automate monitoring.

    #46421. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
    • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
    • GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

    A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

    GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That proposal is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

    Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

    It has been revealed that we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

    Industry observers note that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

    For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

    It has been revealed that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

    This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

    Industry observers note that these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

    To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

    We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

    Two design choices shaped the work:.

    According to recent reports, we compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

    Sources indicate that distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

    Sources indicate that all numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

    No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

    A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That claims nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It demonstrates how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

    In a recent development, linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

    Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

    In a recent development, catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

    Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

    Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

    One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

    Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

    Industry observers note that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

    Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

    Sources indicate that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

    In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can strategy around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

    What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

    Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

    Sources indicate that the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

    Dharma-AI R&D · We Make AI Your Model.

    #46419. Industry News: Your table grew 44 columns after row one: auditing schema drift before it rewrites your backtest

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Your table grew 44 columns after row one: auditing schema drift before it rewrites your backtest

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, A prediction log looks like a stable object.
    • Here is the same table, read honestly.
    • Every one of those facts changes what a WHERE clause means, and none appear in the query you wrote six weeks ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, A prediction log looks like a stable object. You query it, you get numbers, the numbers move when the model changes. That is the story you tell yourself.

    Here is the same table, read honestly. ai_predictions holds 48,737 rows written between 2026-06-21 and 2026-11-21, across 130 columns. Eight of those columns have never held a single value. Forty-four were born after the first row was inserted. Eleven stopped being written before this month began.

    Every one of those facts changes what a WHERE clause means, and none appear in the query you wrote six weeks ago.

    All counts are from production, not an example schema.

    Sources indicate that postgres knows which columns exist. It does not know when each one started carrying data, or whether it still does. That is one pass over the catalog plus one aggregate per column, and you cannot write it as a single static SELECT because a column name cannot be a parameter. Build one statement per column: on 48k rows the sweep takes about 90 seconds.

    Eight dead columns out of 130 is 6.2% of the schema. Four — eu_band, eu_band_hit_baseline, direction_gate, gate_reason — read like a band-based gating feature that was designed, migrated, and never wired up. They document an intention, not behaviour.

    Grouping all 122 written columns by the month of their first non-null value gives the shape of the project rather than the shape of the data. Seventy-eight were present on day one.

    Sources indicate that the 12 that landed in late June are typical: goal_line_direction, training_word_version, opening_assessment, dtl_at. The 13 in August are the second-market block plus the veto experiment. October's two are free-text reasoning fields. Each is a legitimate feature; each also carved a hole. Before the feature existed the column is null, and a null in a column that was not yet born is indistinguishable from a null in a column that was measured and came back empty.

    According to recent reports, that is the whole problem in one sentence. NULL means three different things and Postgres has one symbol for it:.

    Industry observers note that only the third is a bug. The first is your history. If you cannot tell them apart, you cannot audit anything.

    Sources indicate that ah_v5_p_up is the probability output of a v5 scoring pass. Count non-null rows per month:.

    The column was added in July. It became real in October. Between those two facts, 5,536 rows were written and 1 of them carries the v5 value.

    So WHERE ah_v5_p_up IS NOT NULL GROUP BY month returns a table whose first three rows are empty. Not an error, not a warning. An empty result that looks like "v5 had no disagreements in June", when v5 did not exist in June. Anyone reading the output without the row counts beside it will draw the wrong conclusion, and the conclusion will be self-consistent.

    The fix is not a filter, it is a habit: never publish a monthly series without the denominator next to it, and never let a filter quietly reduce the denominator to zero.

    The second failure is worse: the column is present and populated the whole time.

    According to recent reports, ah_tier exists from the first row and holds 46,826 values. It is a small integer severity bucket. Filter ah_tier >= 3 and measure the settlement rate per month:.

    The column is not null in June. The value is simply never 3 or higher. The tier assignment logic that produces 3+ went live in September, so the filter returns zero rows for the first three months and then jumps to a +6.35pp lift.

    Read that as a result and you conclude the tier rule has predictive value. Read it as a schema event and you conclude the tier rule has no June comparison at all — and the +6.35pp is measured against a September baseline that is itself 4.12pp below June's 62.30%. The filtered September slice, 64.53%, is only 2.23pp above the unfiltered June number it is being quietly compared to. Two things changed at once: the population and the pipeline.

    This is the failure mode I care about most, because no invariant catches it. ah_tier is non-null, in range, type-correct — and incomparable across the boundary where its generating rule changed. Only the month × filter cross-tab exposes it.

    According to recent reports, not every later column is a hole. Two of them behave completely differently.

    confidence_calibrated sits at 98–100% fill in every month back to June. That is not plausible for a later addition — the value was recomputed and written back over the whole history. A backfill.

    training_word_version shows a different signature:.

    Nine percent is the fingerprint of a pipeline emitting the field incidentally — some code path that happened to serialize the object. The jump to 92% in August is deliberate adoption. Nothing before August can be segmented by training word version, and no backfill is possible: you cannot reconstruct which word a model carried eight weeks ago if nobody wrote it down.

    Both columns pass a naive count(*) completeness check. Only the monthly breakdown indicates which history is real.

    That gives a usable classification from two queries:.

    hit_veto_ss is the interesting one: 26,731 rows accumulated over two months, then switched off on the last day of October. A dashboard built on it still renders — frozen denominator, flat trend line, forever. Nobody gets an alert because the query does not fail.

    Industry observers note that the defect isn't that the schema changed. It's that the change was invisible at query time. So make it visible.

    Recent findings suggest that call it for every month before you plot it. Here, assert_available(cur, 'ai_predictions', 'ah_v5_p_up', '2026-06') raises on 0/2,735 and the chart never gets built. The failure moves from "a reader interprets a blank as a zero" to "the job crashes at 03:00 naming the column and the month". That is the trade you want.

    A registry makes the same knowledge durable rather than tribal:.

    It has been revealed that populate it from the inventory query and review the diff monthly. A column flipping from forward_only to abandoned is a change worth a ticket; one flipping to never_used after six months should be dropped from the schema instead of confusing the next reader.

    Three numbers, same database, same day: 130 columns declared, 122 ever written; 44 with no history before their birth date; 11 that stopped before this month began.

    According to recent reports, none of these are data-quality problems in the sense of wrong values. Every value that exists is correct. The defect is temporal: the shape of the record changed while the analyses kept treating it as one continuous population.

    If you take one thing: NULL is not a value, it is a timestamp. Before you group by it, ask when that column started, when it stopped, and whether the WHERE clause you inherited is filtering rows — or filtering history.

    Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
    • According to recent reports, the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
    • In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

    The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

    According to recent reports, the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

    In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

    After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

    The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

    Industry observers note that daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

    Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

    Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

    In a recent development, we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

    We selected tasks using three criteria:.

    RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

    57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

    2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

    Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

    Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

    Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

    Industry observers note that our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

    The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

    Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

    Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

    Sources indicate that we’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

    According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

    Cost-Effective Generative AI Development on Azure

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, your generative AI development pipeline is scaling from a handful of test runs to thousands of daily requests, and the Azure bill has jumped from predictable to alarming.
    • It has been revealed that in this guide you will build a cost-aware architecture that still meets latency and throughput targets.
    • Rule of thumb: start with an AML managed cluster for training; spin up an NC v3 VM only when an ad-hoc inference spike exceeds the cluster’s headroom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, your generative AI development pipeline is scaling from a handful of test runs to thousands of daily requests, and the Azure bill has jumped from predictable to alarming. The root cause isn’t a lack of compute power—it’s a cascade of hidden charges in storage, networking, and auto-scaling policies that you never tuned.

    It has been revealed that in this guide you will build a cost-aware architecture that still meets latency and throughput targets. We’ll walk through designing a scalable pipeline on Azure, picking the right services for training and inference, and applying concrete billing hacks that trim compute spend without throttling performance. You’ll also learn how to manage data and model artifacts to avoid storage surprises, and set up monitoring, alerting, and governance rules that keep spend predictable month over month. Follow the steps and you’ll turn an exploding cloud bill into a controlled, repeatable expense model.

    Rule of thumb: start with an AML managed cluster for training; spin up an NC v3 VM only when an ad-hoc inference spike exceeds the cluster’s headroom. For steady-state inference, deploy a low-cost AKS node pool (e.g., Standard NC6s v3) and let the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) drive scaling.

    Gotcha: Premium Files incur higher per-GB cost; limit the cache to the latest model version and purge older checkpoints automatically (e.g., az storage file delete-batch).

    Create a Metric Alert on CPU/GPU utilization and container exit codes. Example JSON for an AKS pod-failure alert:.

    According to recent reports, link the alert to an Azure Automation Runbook that runs kubectl rollout restart deployment/ or scales the VMSS back up. For AML compute, enable auto-heal in the cluster definition (maxNodeCount, idleSecondsBeforeScaleDown).

    Recent findings suggest that instrument each container with the Application Insights SDK (opentelemetry-instrumentation-azure-monitor). Export trace IDs through HTTP headers (traceparent) so the request chain from API gateway → inference pod → downstream data fetch appears in a single view.

    It has been revealed that in the Azure portal, create a Live Metrics Stream filtered on operation_Name = "GenerateText" to spot latency spikes. Use the Performance blade to drill down to the specific function (e.g., tokenizer, GPU kernel) that is the bottleneck.

    Tip: Turn on sampling (5 % default) in production; increase to 100 % in a staging environment to avoid missing rare failure patterns.

    *Cost reflects typical Azure pricing for a 4-core, 16 GiB workload; actual spend varies with region and reserved instances.

    By matching the service to the workload’s performance envelope and your team’s ops bandwidth, you avoid over-provisioning while keeping the generative AI pipeline responsive and cost-controlled.

    When the HPA reports < 30 % GPU utilization for the configured scaleDownUnneededTime, the autoscaler terminates idle nodes, cutting compute spend instantly.

    Tip: Combine a Savings Plan for the bulk of your training workload with RIs for the handful of always-on inference VMs. This hybrid approach maximizes discount depth while preserving the ability to shift workloads between VM families.

    Iterate until the pod’s utilization hovers around 60-80 % of its request; this avoids over-provisioning while keeping headroom for spikes.

    By layering Spot VMs, aggressive AKS auto-scale policies, strategic Savings Plans/RIs, and data-driven container right-sizing, you can shave 50 %+ off your generative AI compute bill without compromising model throughput.

    Gotcha: Cool tier incurs a minimum storage duration (30 days). Deleting a blob before that window incurs a prorated charge, so pair the tier with a lifecycle rule that respects the same 30-day window.

    Training pipelines often pull the same base model (e.g., a fine-tuned LLaMA checkpoint) dozens of times. Store the checkpoint once in Blob Storage, then pull it into Azure Cache for Redis (Standard tier) at pipeline start.

    Gotcha: Redis memory is priced per GB-hour. Keep the cached model size under the cache’s capacity; otherwise Azure will evict older keys, forcing a fallback to Blob reads.

    When training on terabytes of tabular logs or feature tables, Data Lake Gen2 gives you:.

    Industry observers note that create a dedicated Gen2 account, enable secure transfer required, and store each logical dataset in its own folder (/raw/, /processed/). This layout lets you set granular lifecycle policies per folder.

    Azure cost analysis works only if resources carry meaningful metadata.

    Tag every storage account, container, and Redis cache with:.

    Use Azure Policy to enforce the tag set on creation – otherwise orphaned resources silently inflate the bill.

    The following policy moves blobs from Cool to Archive after 30 days and deletes them after 365 days. Apply it at the container level.

    Implementation tip: Deploy the policy via Azure CLI:.

    Gotcha: Lifecycle actions run on a daily schedule, so expect up to 24 hours lag before a blob actually transitions or is removed. Align your data retention windows accordingly to avoid accidental deletions.

    In a recent development, gotcha: Budgets are evaluated against actual spend, not forecasts. If you rely on reserved instances, include the amortized cost in the budget calculation; otherwise the budget will fire prematurely.

    Apply tags at resource creation (e.g., az vm create … --tags Project=GenAI-Chatbot Env=Prod Owner=jdoe). Enforce tagging with an Azure Policy that denies creation of untagged resources.

    Why: Tag filters appear in Cost Management reports, letting you spot a runaway dev VM that is still tagged Env=Prod.

    In a recent development, enable Advisor recommendations (if not already on) via Advisor → Settings → Enable recommendations. Focus on:.

    Automate remediation: a Logic App can read Advisor’s REST endpoint and matter az vm deallocate or az disk patch --sku Standard_LRS commands.

    Gotcha: Advisor’s idle detection respects the last 30 days only; newly released training nodes will be ignored until they age out.

    Set the dataset refresh to every hour; Power BI will surface spikes before the email budget alert fires.

    In a recent development, restrict Contributor or Owner roles on Azure Machine Learning, Azure Kubernetes Service, and GPU-enabled VMs. Instead, grant:.

    Run a weekly Access Review (Azure AD → Governance → Access reviews) to confirm that only the intended groups hold these roles. Export the role assignments to CSV and compare against the tag Owner field; mismatches indicate orphaned privileges that could lead to uncontrolled spin-ups.

    By combining budgets, enforced tagging, Advisor cleanup, a live Power BI view, and tight RBAC, you keep generative-AI spend visible and under control without throttling model performance.

    Spot VMs can be reclaimed with short notice, so training jobs may be interrupted. Azure ML pipelines can checkpoint state and automatically resubmit on a different node, mitigating impact. For workloads tolerant to preemption—large batch epochs, hyperparameter sweeps—Spot offers up to 80% cost reduction. Critical, time-bound training should stay on regular VMs or use a mixed strategy with Spot for non-essential phases.

    It has been revealed that choose Azure ML managed compute when you need quick provisioning, built-in model versioning, and auto-scaling based on request latency, without managing Kubernetes clusters. It’s ideal for standard REST endpoints, A/B testing, and workloads under a few hundred concurrent requests. AKS becomes preferable if you require custom networking, multi-model serving on the same node, or integration with existing container orchestration pipelines. In short, let managed compute handle most inference; reserve AKS for complex, highly-customized deployments.

    Recent findings suggest that adopt a flat tag hierarchy: Project, Owner, Environment, CostCenter, AIComponent, and Version. Apply tags at resource group level so all child resources inherit them. Enforce via Azure Policy to reject creation without required tags. Use consistent values (e.g., “dev”, “prod”) and avoid free-form text that fragments reporting. Integrate tags with Azure Cost Management to generate component-level dashboards, and review them weekly to catch orphaned or mis-tagged resources before they inflate the bill.

    According to recent reports, yes, you can layer Savings Looks on top of Spot VMs, but the effect is limited. Savings Plans apply to the base compute rate, while Spot already discounts the on-demand price. When you reserve a Savings Strategy for a VM family, Spot instances of that family still receive the Spot discount, effectively giving you the Spot price plus the plan’s commitment discount. The net saving is modest; evaluate whether the added commitment complexity is worth the incremental reduction.

    Building a generative AI solution on Azure starts with a disciplined architecture: choose the right compute tier, automate cost-aware scaling, and enforce tagging and monitoring from day one. By applying Spot VMs for non-critical training, leveraging Azure Machine Learning managed compute for most inference, and using lifecycle policies for data, you can keep the bill predictable while delivering production-grade performance.     #46414. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3839 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
    • Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
    • Sources indicate that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

    Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

    Sources indicate that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

    Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) demonstrated that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

    It has been revealed that we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

    According to recent reports, most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

    For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

    RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

    According to recent reports, this section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

    According to recent reports, each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

    We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

    According to recent reports, A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

    According to recent reports, each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

    According to recent reports, 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

    According to recent reports, A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

    Sources indicate that of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below highlights how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

    According to recent reports, qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

    It has been revealed that this example demonstrates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

    It has been revealed that the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

    Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

    The figure below reveals how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

    Industry observers note that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below highlights what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

    We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

    For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

    Recent findings suggest that to obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

    The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which indicated that 0.1 worked best).

    In a recent development, we performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

    Industry observers note that each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below indicates the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

    As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

    Industry observers note that the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

    According to recent reports, before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

    According to recent reports, we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

    Industry observers note that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

    Sources indicate that merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

    Recent findings suggest that we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

    Industry observers note that we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each revision below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

    The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own revision. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

    Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

    In a recent development, "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

    With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

    Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

    Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

    According to recent reports, the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

    Industry observers note that the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

    This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

    Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

    Industry observers note that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

    On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

    This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

    It has been revealed that we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

    In a recent development, every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

    For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

    For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

    Recent findings suggest that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

    The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

    To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

    Recent findings suggest that under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

    What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

    We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

    Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

    We appreciate the feedback from the owners and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

    In a recent development, this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

    Recent findings suggest that this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

    Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

    In a recent development, however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

    Sources indicate that throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

    In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

    According to recent reports, we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

    In a recent development, thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

    #46413. NVIDIA's Workday Search Stated 2,000 Jobs. Its Own Filter Counts Added Up to 2,645

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1076 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    NVIDIA's Workday Search Stated 2,000 Jobs. Its Own Filter Counts Added Up to 2,645

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I run a visa agency in Bali and build scrapers on Apify on the side.
    • Workday is a pleasant target compared to most job boards.
    • Open any Workday career page with the network tab open and you will see the page call itself:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I run a visa agency in Bali and build scrapers on Apify on the side. One of them reads Workday career sites — the firm.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com pages that NVIDIA, Salesforce, Adobe and a long list of banks and retailers use to publish openings. My own reason for caring is simple: when a company starts hiring a lot in Indonesia, somebody there will soon need a work permit.

    Workday is a pleasant target compared to most job boards. There is no login, no browser needed, and every tenant runs the same JSON API. But on 21 November 2026 I noticed that the number the API reports as total is not the number of jobs on the site. This post is about that, plus the other things I had to learn before the rows came out clean.

    Open any Workday career page with the network tab open and you will see the page call itself:.

    Sources indicate that the path is /wday/cxs///jobs. The tenant is the first label of the host (nvidia), the site is the first path segment after an optional locale like en-US. Each job in the response has an externalPath, and a GET on /wday/cxs// returns the full posting: description HTML, time type, country, additional locations, requisition id, the date it went live.

    Two things I learned by getting them wrong:.

    Here is what NVIDIA's endpoint answered on 21 November:.

    It has been revealed that same number for "everything" and for one keyword. That alone is suspicious. The first page of the response also carries facets — the filters you see on the left of the career page — with a count for every value. Summing the jobFamilyGroup facet:.

    Three independent facets agree on 2,645. For "engineer" the job-family facet summed to 2,516, against a total of 2,000.

    So I paged past the ceiling to see what happens:.

    No error, no empty page — past 2,000 the endpoint hands you page one again. A scraper that trusts total stops at 2,000 and misses 645 jobs. A scraper that ignores total and keeps going until the page is empty never stops, and fills your dataset with duplicates.

    According to recent reports, the fix is the facets themselves. Filtering by one job family brings the count under the ceiling, and then total is honest:.

    According to recent reports, that returned total: 1641 — exactly the Engineering facet count. Split by job family, page each slice, de-duplicate by externalPath, and you get the whole site.

    One caution: facet sums are only a good estimate when a job can sit in one value. On Salesforce the first facet is the posting country; it summed to 1,643 while total said 1,614, because a job open in two countries counts twice. Adobe's external site was small enough that both said 253. The ceiling only bites on significant tenants.

    Honest status of my own tool: today the Workday Jobs Scraper follows total and de-duplicates, so it stops cleanly at 2,000 per search — no duplicates, but also no job 2,001. Splitting by facet when total hits exactly 2,000 is the next change. If you need more than 2,000 rows from one employer before then, run several keywords: each search has its own ceiling.

    The last run before I wrote this was the default example: NVIDIA, keyword "engineer", 40 jobs, full postings on.

    It finished in about 25 seconds, made 43 HTTP requests (two search pages, 40 postings, one for the company name) and charged $0.054. One row, trimmed:.

    The median description was about 3,600 characters of plain text, with the HTML kept next to it.

    postedOn is a label, not a date. The search returns "Posted Yesterday", "Posted 4 Days Ago", "Posted 30+ Days Ago". In those 40 rows, 17 mentioned "30+ Days Ago". The posting endpoint has the real startDate, and for those 17 it ranged from 20 October back to 2 March — anywhere from one month to almost nine months. If you sort by freshness using the label, a March posting and an October one are tied. Take the date from the posting call, which means paying for the second request per job.

    It has been revealed that there is a sharp edge here in my own Actor that I found while writing this: the "posted within N days" filter reads the label, before the posting is fetched, and treats "30+" as 30. With a window of 30 days or less that is fine — "30+" posts drop out. With a 60-day window, a job from March gets in. Until that is fixed, use 30 days or less, or filter on postedAt yourself.

    Industry observers note that hiringOrganization is the legal entity, not the brand. 40 NVIDIA rows named twelve different employers: "2100 NVIDIA USA" (18), "IL00 Mellanox Technologies, Ltd." (9), "IN01 NVIDIA Graphics Bengaluru" (3), and nine more, each with an internal code in front. Nine of the 40 engineering jobs are formally Mellanox, the Israeli company NVIDIA bought years ago. For a recruiter that is noise. For someone working out which local entity will sponsor a visa, it is the most useful field in the row. The Actor keeps it as is and puts the brand from the career page's og:title in company.

    According to recent reports, remoteType was empty on all 40. Twelve of those rows had "Remote" in the location itself ("US, CA, Remote", "Poland, Remote"). NVIDIA simply does not fill the remote field; it encodes remote work as a location. If you filter remote jobs by remoteType, you get zero on this tenant. Check the location strings too.

    Workday sits behind Cloudflare, and its 429 is often not a rate limit but a bot challenge. On 16 November that challenge was triggered by the TLS handshake of a newer Node.js image on every route, residential proxies included; going back to Node 20 passed four requests out of four. If you write your own client and get 429 from the first request, try a different runtime before buying proxies. Workday also puts tenants into scheduled maintenance, mostly at weekends; the API then redirects to a maintenance page instead of returning JSON, and the only fix is to wait.

    The dataset ends with a free type: "notice" row summarizing the run; filter on type == "job".

    The first thing I would check on any Workday tenant now is whether total is exactly 2,000. If it is, the real number is in the facets.

    How I built the recommendation engine behind CineHindi (there is a surprise, click the link and see magic happen)

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (472 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, cineHindi is a movie and TV discovery app I built with Next.js and the TMDB API.
    • Sources indicate that TMDB gives you metadata: titles, posters, genres, ratings, cast.
    • Every movie or show you open, like, or add to your watchlist feeds the engine.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, cineHindi is a movie and TV discovery app I built with Next.js and the TMDB API. It covers Bollywood, South Indian cinema, Hollywood, K-dramas, anime and Indian web series — 28 curated categories in total — and the part I spent the most time on is the bit that decides what to show you next: the recommendation engine.

    Sources indicate that TMDB gives you metadata: titles, posters, genres, ratings, cast. What it does not give you is a reason to pick one row over another. A grid of posters is a catalogue, not a guide. I wanted the home page to feel like it knew what I had been watching, so I built a small scoring engine that runs over the user's own history and re-ranks everything into personal rows: "For You" and "Because You Watched …".

    Every movie or show you open, like, or add to your watchlist feeds the engine. The score for a candidate title comes from three signals:.

    The engine lives in a single module (lib/recommend.ts) and is shared by the browse UI and the API routes, so the rows you see on the home page and the rows the API returns are always scored the same way.

    According to recent reports, signing in is optional, and when you do, your guest library merges into your account. The rule is simple: existing cloud rows win, everything else carries over. Cloud writes are fire-and-forget, so browsing never waits on the network, and every table is locked down with row-level security so a user can only ever read their own rows.

    In a recent development, TV demonstrates remember the last season and episode you opened and jump straight back to it. Playback runs through third-party iframe servers, so resume is tracked at the episode level rather than to the exact second — the schema is ready for position-based resume the moment a player exposes playback events.

    Recent findings suggest that the 28 categories are curated, not auto-generated, and every one of them is shareable: a link like /browse?category=anime&type=all opens exactly that shelf. The discovery UI is ranked rows, carousels, genre pages and live search with filters — all fed by the same scoring.

    Sources indicate that two things. First, I would add position-based resume from the start — episode-level resume is fine, but second-level resume is what people actually expect. Second, I would put the scoring behind a small test suite earlier. The engine is one module with clear inputs and outputs, which is exactly the kind of code that is easy to test and easy to let drift.

    Sources indicate that the repo is open source: github.com/akyourowngames/Movix. If you build something similar, I would love to hear how you score — did you weight recency, or genres, or something else entirely?

    #46411. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2416 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model.
    • Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
    • Industry observers note that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

    Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

    Industry observers note that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

    This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

    Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

    According to recent reports, similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

    Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

    It has been revealed that text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

    In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

    In a recent development, inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

    Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

    In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

    We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

    You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

    According to recent reports, to set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

    In a recent development, pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

    Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

    Let’s get our model to call some tools.

    In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

    If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

    Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

    For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

    Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

    Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.
